title: Review: Basic proofs
description: Questions on the ideas in this guide, from one star (a check of the definitions) to four stars (combining several ideas). They come in a random order each time.

questions.question: Which statement says exactly the same as “if $$3 \mid a^2$$, then $$3 \mid a$$”?
options: If $$3 \mid a$$, then $$3 \mid a^2$$
If $$3 \nmid a^2$$, then $$3 \nmid a$$
If $$3 \nmid a$$, then $$3 \nmid a^2$$
$$3 \mid a$$ and $$3 \mid a^2$$
questions.explanation: Swapping the two parts and denying both gives the contrapositive, which says the same as the original (:ref{#contrapositive-equivalent}); this is how :ref{#numbers/squares-three} is proved. The first option is the converse; it happens to be true, but it is a different statement. The second is the contrapositive of the converse, so it says the same as the first option, not as the original.

questions.question: To prove “$$P$$ exactly when $$Q$$”, what has to be shown?
options: That $$P$$ is true
That $$P$$ leads to $$Q$$
That $$Q$$ leads to $$P$$
That $$P$$ leads to $$Q$$, and $$Q$$ leads to $$P$$
questions.explanation: “Exactly when” claims both directions, so both must be proved (:ref{#exactly-when}), as in the proof of :ref{#numbers/cross-multiplying-rational}.

questions.question: What does a proof by contradiction do?
options: Assumes the statement is false and shows this leads to something impossible
Finds an example where the statement fails
Proves the statement for small cases first
Proves the opposite statement
questions.explanation: That is the pattern of :ref{#contradiction}. For example, :ref{#numbers/sqrt-two} supposes a rational square root of $$2$$ exists and shows its numerator and denominator would have to be both even, which is impossible for a fraction in lowest form.

questions.question: A rule has been checked for a thousand pairs of integers and always works. What does this establish?
options: That it is true for all integers
That it is true for all integers up to a thousand
Only that it holds for those pairs; a proof is needed for every case
That it is probably an axiom
questions.explanation: Checking cases can find a mistake but never covers every integer, and a pattern can hold for many cases and then break. That is why a “for every” claim needs a proof, built from definitions, basic rules and earlier results.

questions.question: How many counterexamples are needed to show that a statement about every integer is false?
options: One
At least two
As many as there are integers
None; such statements can't be disproved
questions.explanation: A single case where the statement fails is enough (:ref{#counterexample}). For example, $$a = b = 1$$ shows that $$(a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2$$ is not true for every $$a$$ and $$b$$.

questions.question: A proof by induction that something holds for every positive integer $$n$$ must show which two things?
options: It holds for $$n = 1$$ and for $$n = 2$$
It holds for $$n = 1$$, and whenever it holds for $$n = k$$ it holds for $$n = k + 1$$
It holds for a large $$n$$, and whenever it holds for $$n = k + 1$$ it holds for $$n = k$$
It holds whenever it holds for $$n = k + 1$$
questions.explanation: Like a row of dominoes: the first one falls, and each one knocks over the next (:ref{#induction}). Without the first case nothing gets started.

questions.question: Which of these is **not yet** a statement?
options: $$15$$ is a multiple of $$4$$
Every whole number is even
$$n$$ is a multiple of $$4$$
$$12$$ is a multiple of $$4$$
questions.explanation: A statement is either true or false (:ref{#statement}). The others are all statements, two of them false. “$$n$$ is a multiple of $$4$$” can't be judged until something is said about $$n$$.

questions.question: Is “$$7$$ is even” a statement?
options: No, because it is false
Yes: it is a false statement, and false statements are still statements
No, because it has no letters in it
Only once it has been proved
questions.explanation: A statement only has to be true or false, not true (:ref{#statement}). “$$7$$ is even” makes a definite claim, which happens to be false.

questions.question: A single example where it works is enough to prove which kind of claim?
options: “For every $$x$$, $$P(x)$$”
“There is no $$x$$ with $$P(x)$$”
None of them; examples never prove anything
“There is an $$x$$ with $$P(x)$$”
questions.explanation: “There is” only claims at least one success, so one example proves it (:ref{#quantifiers}). Examples can't prove a “for every” claim, and one example works against a “there is no” claim.

questions.question: What is the opposite of “every number on the list is even”?
options: Some number on the list is odd
Every number on the list is odd
No number on the list is even
Some number on the list is even
questions.explanation: Denying a “for every” claim gives “there is one for which it fails” (:ref{#statement-negation}). “Every number is odd” is far stronger than needed.

questions.question: Is “there is a number $$x$$ with $$x^2 = 2$$” true?
options: Yes, always
It depends on which numbers are allowed: false among fractions, true among real numbers
No, never
It is not a statement at all
questions.explanation: No fraction squares to $$2$$ (:ref{#numbers/sqrt-two}), but the real number $$\sqrt{2}$$ does. That is why a careful statement says what kind of number each letter is.

questions.question: For a real number $$x$$, why are “$$x = 5$$” and “$$x^2 = 25$$” **not** equivalent?
options: The second has a square in it, so it can't be equivalent to anything without one
Neither leads to the other
The first leads to the second, but $$x = -5$$ makes the second true and the first false
They are equivalent, since $$5^2 = 25$$
questions.explanation: Equivalent statements are true for exactly the same $$x$$ (:ref{#equivalent-statements}). One direction holds, but not the other.

questions.question: Why does “for any numbers $$x$$ and $$y$$, $$\frac{x^2 - y^2}{x - y} = x + y$$” need the word “distinct”?
options: Because different letters must name different numbers
Because the identity is false for every $$x$$ and $$y$$
It doesn't; the statement is true as it stands
“Any numbers $$x$$ and $$y$$” includes $$x = y$$, where the left side divides by $$0$$
questions.explanation: Different letters can name the same number, so a statement about “any $$x$$ and $$y$$” covers $$x = y$$. Saying “distinct” rules that case out, and then the identity holds.

questions.question: What does “solve $$x^2 = 9$$” ask for?
options: Every number $$x$$ with $$x^2 = 9$$, and a reason there are no others
One number that works, such as $$3$$
The positive answer only
A check that $$3^2 = 9$$
questions.explanation: Solving means finding every solution: $$x = 3$$ or $$x = -3$$, with a reason there are no more.

questions.question: Which of these can justify a step in a proof?
options: It works for every example tried
It looks true on a diagram
Most people believe it
A result proved earlier
questions.explanation: Every step must follow from a definition, a basic rule taken as given, or a result proved earlier. Examples, pictures and opinion don't settle every case.

questions.question: To prove that the sum of two even numbers is even, why write them as $$2k$$ and $$2l$$ rather than $$2k$$ and $$2k$$?
options: $$k$$ must always be odd
Using $$k$$ twice would only cover the case where the two numbers are equal
It makes no difference to the proof
Each letter can only be used once on a page
questions.explanation: The two even numbers could be anything, so each needs its own letter. Writing both as $$2k$$ quietly assumes they are the same number.

questions.question: A proof about every integer splits into the cases “positive” and “negative”. What is wrong?
options: The cases miss $$0$$, so the proof doesn't cover every integer
Nothing; two cases are always enough
Proofs can't be split into cases
The negative case is never needed
questions.explanation: A proof by cases must cover every possibility. $$0$$ is neither positive nor negative, so it needs its own case or must join one of the others.

questions.question: A proof by contradiction reaches $$1 = 2$$, but one of its steps divided by a number that might be $$0$$. What has it shown?
options: That the statement is true
That the statement is false
Nothing: the impossible result may come from the faulty step, not from the supposition
questions.explanation: :ref{#contradiction} blames the supposition, so every other step has to be valid. A faulty step could be the real cause.

questions.question: How do you prove “there is an even prime number”?
options: Check every even number
Show that no odd number is prime
It can't be proved, only checked
Give one: $$2$$ is even and prime
questions.explanation: A “there is” claim needs only one example (:ref{#quantifiers}). It is “for every” claims that examples can't prove.

questions.question: “If you score over $$90$$, then you get an A.” What does this say about someone who scores $$80$$?
options: Nothing: it only promises an A when the score is over $$90$$
They don't get an A
They do get an A
The statement is false
questions.explanation: “If $$P$$, then $$Q$$” promises $$Q$$ whenever $$P$$ holds, and says nothing when $$P$$ fails.

questions.question: “If $$x > 2$$, then $$x^2 > 4$$” is true. Which value shows that its converse is false?
options: None; the converse of a true statement is true
questions.explanation: The converse is “if $$x^2 > 4$$, then $$x > 2$$” (:ref{#contrapositive}). At $$x = -3$$, $$x^2 = 9 > 4$$ but $$x$$ is not bigger than $$2$$.

questions.question: Which statement says the same as “if it rains, the ground gets wet”?
options: If the ground is wet, it rained
If the ground is not wet, it didn't rain
If it doesn't rain, the ground doesn't get wet
It rains exactly when the ground gets wet
questions.explanation: That is the contrapositive, which stands or falls with the original (:ref{#contrapositive-equivalent}). The first is the converse, and the second is the contrapositive of the converse; a hose could wet the ground without rain.

questions.question: What does “$$n$$ is a multiple of $$4$$ only if $$n$$ is even” mean?
options: If $$n$$ is even, then $$n$$ is a multiple of $$4$$
$$n$$ is a multiple of $$4$$ exactly when $$n$$ is even
$$n$$ is never a multiple of $$4$$
If $$n$$ is a multiple of $$4$$, then $$n$$ is even
questions.explanation: “$$P$$ only if $$Q$$” means “if $$P$$, then $$Q$$”: $$P$$ can't happen without $$Q$$. Reading it the other way round gives the converse, which is false here, since $$6$$ is even but not a multiple of $$4$$.

questions.question: Which phrase means “if $$Q$$, then $$P$$”?
options: $$P$$ only if $$Q$$
If $$P$$, then $$Q$$
$$P$$ if and only if $$Q$$
questions.explanation: In “$$P$$ if $$Q$$”, the condition is $$Q$$. “$$P$$ only if $$Q$$” is the other direction, and “if and only if” is both (:ref{#exactly-when}).

questions.question: Why isn't it circular to assume $$P(k)$$ in the inductive step?
options: Because $$P(k)$$ has already been checked for every $$k$$
It is circular, but induction allows it
Because the step only proves “if $$P(k)$$, then $$P(k + 1)$$”, not $$P(k)$$ itself
Because $$k$$ is always $$1$$
questions.explanation: The step proves a link between neighbouring cases (:ref{#induction}). Only the base case and the chain of links together make every case true.

questions.question: For $$P(n)$$: “$$n = n + 1$$”, the inductive step works: from $$k = k + 1$$, adding $$1$$ gives $$k + 1 = k + 2$$. What has been proved?
options: That $$n = n + 1$$ for every $$n$$
Nothing, because the base case $$1 = 2$$ is false
That $$n = n + 1$$ for large $$n$$
That induction doesn't work
questions.explanation: Without a base case nothing gets started: the step only passes truth along, and here there is none to pass (:ref{#induction}).

questions.question: To prove $$2^n > n^2$$ for every $$n \ge 5$$ by induction, what changes?
options: The base case is $$n = 5$$, and the step may assume $$k \ge 5$$
Nothing; the base case is still $$n = 1$$
The step must also work from $$k = 2$$ to $$k = 3$$
Induction can't be used, since the claim fails for $$n = 2$$
questions.explanation: The chain starts at $$5$$, so the step is only ever used from $$5$$ onwards, and the fact that $$k \ge 5$$ is available in it.

questions.question: An inductive step reaches $$P(k + 1)$$ without using $$P(k)$$ anywhere. What does that suggest?
options: The proof is especially strong
The base case can be skipped
$$P(k)$$ must be false
Either the statement didn't need induction, or something has gone wrong
questions.explanation: The point of the step is to use $$P(k)$$ to reach $$P(k + 1)$$. If it was never used, check the argument; a correct one could have proved $$P(n)$$ directly.

questions.question: Which is true of $$\{1, 2\}$$, $$\{2, 1\}$$ and $$\{1, 1, 2\}$$?
options: They are three different sets
Only the first two are the same
They are all the same set
Only the first and last are the same
questions.explanation: A set is decided by its elements (:ref{#set}); order and repeats don't count.

questions.question: Which pair of statements is correct?
questions.explanation: A number is an element, written with $$\in$$; a set is a subset, written with $$\subseteq$$ (:ref{#subset}). The elements of $$\{1, 2, 3\}$$ are numbers, not sets.

questions.question: How is $$\varnothing$$ different from $$\{0\}$$?
options: $$\varnothing$$ has no elements, while $$\{0\}$$ has one, the number $$0$$
They are the same set
$$\{0\}$$ has no elements, while $$\varnothing$$ has one
$$\varnothing$$ is a number and $$\{0\}$$ is a set
questions.explanation: The empty set has nothing in it (:ref{#empty-set}). $$\{0\}$$ is a bag holding one thing, which happens to be zero.

questions.question: Why is $$\varnothing$$ a subset of every set $$A$$?
options: Because $$A$$ always contains $$0$$
It isn't; only $$\varnothing \subseteq \varnothing$$
Because every set has $$\varnothing$$ as an element
To fail, it would need an element outside $$A$$, and it has no elements at all
questions.explanation: $$\varnothing \subseteq A$$ says every element of $$\varnothing$$ is in $$A$$, and there is nothing that could break it (:ref{#set-empty-subset}).

questions.question: To prove two sets $$A$$ and $$B$$ are equal, what has to be shown?
options: $$A \subseteq B$$ only
That they have one element in common
$$A \subseteq B$$ and $$B \subseteq A$$
That they are described by the same test
questions.explanation: Equal sets have exactly the same elements, which is both inclusions together (:ref{#set-equality}). A small set can sit inside a big one without being equal to it.

questions.question: What is $$\{x : 0 < x < 4\}$$?
options: It depends on where $$x$$ comes from: $$\{1, 2, 3\}$$ among the integers, an interval among the real numbers
Always the interval $$(0, 4)$$
The empty set
questions.explanation: A set given by a test should say what kind of object is allowed in, as in $$\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : 0 < x < 4\}$$, because that changes the answer.

questions.question: Solving an equation, the working gives a list of candidates, and then each candidate is checked. In terms of sets, what does each half show?
options: The working shows the solution set is a subset of the list; the check shows the list is a subset of the solution set
The working shows the list is a subset of the solution set; the check is only for arithmetic slips
Both halves show the same inclusion
Neither half is about sets
questions.explanation: Together the two inclusions make the list exactly the solution set (:ref{#set-equality}). Steps such as squaring can add candidates, which is why the check matters.

questions.question: What does $$x_2$$ mean?
options: $$x$$ times $$2$$
$$x$$ squared
The second term of a list $$x_1, x_2, \dots$$
questions.explanation: A subscript is a label saying which number in the list is meant, not an operation.

questions.question: In “let $$x_1, x_2, x_3$$ be numbers”, can $$x_1$$ and $$x_2$$ be equal?
options: No; different subscripts always mean different numbers
Only if $$x_3$$ is equal to them too
Only if they are whole numbers
Yes; different subscripts are just different names
questions.explanation: As with different letters, different subscripts don't promise different values (:ref{#sequence}).

questions.question: How many terms does $$\sum_{i=3}^{8} x_i$$ add up?
questions.explanation: The index runs through $$3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$$ (:ref{#sum-notation}). From $$m$$ to $$n$$ there are $$n - m + 1$$ terms, not $$n - m$$.

questions.question: Is $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$$ the same as $$\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j$$?
options: Yes: the index of summation only has a meaning inside the sum, so it can be renamed
No; $$i$$ and $$j$$ are different numbers
Only when $$n = 1$$
Only if $$i = j$$ is stated first
questions.explanation: The index is a placeholder that runs through the values (:ref{#sum-notation}); any unused letter does the same job.

questions.question: Is $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i$$ always equal to $$\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i\right)$$?
options: Yes, by the rules for sums
Yes, because multiplication is commutative
Only when every $$x_i$$ is $$0$$
No: with $$n = 2$$ and every term $$1$$, the left side is $$2$$ and the right side is $$4$$
questions.explanation: Sums split over $$+$$ and constant factors come out (:ref{#notation-sum-rules}), but a sum of products is not a product of sums; one counterexample (:ref{#counterexample}) settles it.

questions.question: Why should every letter be introduced before it is used?
options: Because each letter can only be used once
So the reader knows what kind of thing it is, and whether the claim is about every value or just some
So that it can be given a numerical value
It doesn't matter as long as the answer is right
questions.explanation: A letter from nowhere leaves the reader guessing (:ref{#notation-introduce}). Introducing it also fixes the quantifier (:ref{#quantifiers}).
